subtopics.title: What a GIS Is — Layers of Information

questions.question: A Geographical Information System is best defined as:
options: A satellite that photographs the earth
A paper atlas stored in a library
A computerised system that captures, stores, analyses and displays geographically referenced information
A GPS receiver in a car

questions.question: A spreadsheet of clinic names becomes geographical information when:
options: Each clinic carries coordinates tying it to a position on the earth's surface
It is printed in colour
It is sorted alphabetically
It is emailed to a planner

questions.question: Overlay analysis means:
options: Printing a map on transparent paper
Stacking georeferenced layers so questions can be answered by combining them — such as finding dense settlement far from clinics
Tracing a map by hand
Deleting old layers from the database

questions.question: For a school stored in a GIS, its position is the spatial data, while its name, learner numbers and language of instruction are:
options: Metadata errors
A separate layer
Raster data
Attribute data linked to the feature

subtopics.title: The Five Components of a GIS

questions.question: The five components of a GIS are:
options: Hardware, software, data, people and procedures
Satellites, aircraft, drones, balloons and towers
Maps, globes, atlases, photographs and charts
Keyboards, screens, printers, mice and cables

questions.question: Data is called the most important and most expensive component because:
options: Computers cannot store very much of it
It must be bought from other countries
Without accurate, up-to-date georeferenced data, even the best hardware and software produce misleading results
It is protected by copyright

questions.question: The procedures component of a GIS covers:
options: The electrical wiring of the computers
The rules for checking data, updating layers and verifying accuracy
The satellites that capture images
The printing of final maps

questions.question: Census results from Statistics South Africa enter GIS work as:
options: Software used to draw maps
Hardware for the counting teams
A procedure for training operators
Data feeding the layers used for planning

questions.question: Remote sensing is:
options: Measuring rainfall with gauges on the ground
Gathering information about the earth's surface from a distance, without physical contact, using sensors on satellites or aircraft
Interviewing people by telephone
Using a compass to find direction

questions.question: Sensors can reveal things invisible to the human eye because they:
options: Zoom in more than any camera
Fly closer to the ground
Read wavelengths such as infrared, in which stressed crops and soil moisture show up
Photograph only at night

questions.question: Compared with aerial photographs, satellite images:
options: Cover far larger areas and revisit the same spot on a fixed cycle, building a time series
Show finer detail over smaller areas
Are always free of cloud problems
Are taken from a lower altitude

questions.question: A key limitation of remote sensing for population studies is that it:
options: Cannot photograph cities
Only works in the southern hemisphere
Cannot detect change over time
Counts roofs, not names — it cannot ask who lives in a dwelling, so the ground census remains essential

subtopics.title: Satellites, Aerial Photographs and Population Work

questions.question: Satellite images help planners serve informal settlements by:
options: Recording residents' names and ages
Replacing the need for water and clinics
Showing new roof clusters appearing between censuses, which become a GIS layer overlaid with service layers
Predicting the weather for the settlement

questions.question: Before a census, Statistics South Africa uses aerial and satellite imagery to:
options: Divide the country into small counting areas so no dwelling is missed
Count the population automatically from space
Estimate incomes from roof sizes
Replace enumerators with drones

questions.question: During the April 2022 KwaZulu-Natal floods, before-and-after satellite images were valuable because they:
options: Stopped the rain from falling
Identified destroyed neighbourhoods and cut roads while the ground was still impassable
Rebuilt the damaged bridges
Warned residents a year in advance

questions.question: South Africa's national space agency, which receives satellite data at Hartebeesthoek, is:
options: NASA
ESA
SAWS
SANSA

subtopics.title: The Smartphone Map You Already Use

questions.question: In the pizza-search example, the analysis step of the GIS definition is performed when:
options: The screen lights up
The phone connects to the internet
The application works out the nearest pizza place and the streets connecting it to you
The pizza is ordered

questions.question: In the smartphone example, the people component of the GIS is:
options: The user asking the question and choosing the answer
The phone's battery
The red pins on the map
The satellite overhead

questions.question: Tapping a pin to open a shop's name, menu and rating demonstrates:
options: Overlay analysis of two layers
The link between spatial data — the position — and attribute data — the description
Remote sensing from orbit
The hardware component

questions.question: In the transparent-sheets picture, one sheet showing only rivers represents:
options: The attribute table
The hardware of the GIS
A single thematic layer, georeferenced to the same ground as the other sheets
A satellite image

questions.question: Stacking the density, clinic and road sheets reveals an underserved community because:
options: The sheets change colour when stacked
Rivers always flow past clinics
Each sheet answers the question on its own
Dense population shading appears where the clinic layer shows nothing — a combination no single sheet could show

questions.question: A five-year-old clinic layer is dangerous in a GIS because:
options: The analysis will look convincing while recommending decisions based on outdated reality
Old layers take up too much memory
The computer refuses to load old data
Clinics cannot be mapped after five years

subtopics.title: The Eye in the Sky and the Census

questions.question: Lining up satellite images of the same place over months and years allows analysts to:
options: Hear sounds from the ground
Detect change — a shrinking dam, a creeping city edge, a changing coastline
Measure the temperature of the sensor
Remove clouds from the sky

questions.question: South Africa's 1 to 10 000 orthophoto maps are built from:
options: Hand-drawn sketches
Weather radar
Corrected aerial photographs taken from aircraft, detailed enough to show single houses
Images from deep-space telescopes

questions.question: Healthy crops can be told apart from struggling crops across a whole province because:
options: Farmers paint healthy fields
Satellites fly lower over farmland
Struggling crops grow taller
Healthy plants reflect strongly in infrared, which sensors read but eyes cannot

questions.question: The lesson's closing point about the satellite and the census enumerator is that:
options: The satellite sees everywhere but the person at the door asks everything — each needs the other
Satellites will soon replace the census entirely
Enumerators no longer use maps
The census only counts urban areas
